newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Ex-minister says NZ First-National deal unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Ex-minister says NZ First-National deal unlikely.

text.p: Outgoing Trade Negotiations Minister Philip Burdon said on Monday the chances of nationalist New Zealand First Party forming a coalition with the conservative National Party were "minimal".

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who was dumped from the National Cabinet by Prime Minister Jim Bolger in 1991, holds the balance of power after Saturday's general election, but has not indicated which way he will jump.
Most commentators before the election expected him to opt for Labour.
Writing in the "Evening Post" newspaper, Burdon said : "The spectacle of Winston Peters and Michael Laws as the white knights who ensure the National Party retain control of power is ridiculous."
Laws left National to join New Zealand First earlier this year and is now Peters' leading strategist.

"They both deeply resent the treatment they received at the hands of the National caucus and in personal and philosophic terms will be relishing the opportunity to embarrass many of their former colleagues.

"The price of a coalition deal which compromises the Reserve Bank Act, privatisation, the Employment Contracts Act, foreign investment and immigration policy would be seen as betraying the integrity of the reforms of the past six years," Burdon said.
He said Peters would go through the motions of negotiations "but nothing will happen".
Bolger said he had not read Burdon's article.
"Philip has resigned and I guess his views are now those of an individual outside parliament," Bolger said.
Bolger said he had not yet reallocated the portfolios held by Burdon, who by law remains a minister for another month.

The ruling National Party won 44 seats in the 120 seat parliament at the general election on Saturday, but with its allies, free-market Act New Zealand and the sole United Party MP it can commmand only 53 seats.
On the left Labour won 37 seats on the night and the left wing Alliance 13, leaving New Zealand holding the balance of power with 17 seats.
Both Bolger and Labour leader Helen Clark have indicated they want to form a government with Peters' support.
